analysis.one_liner: Bars large investment funds from buying single-family homes and requires them to sell off existing holdings over ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced January 22, 2026, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since its first day with no hearing, no vote, and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Investment Company Act of 1940 to bar large investment funds — private funds, registered investment companies, and real estate investment trusts with more than $500 million in assets, or those owning 100 or more single-family homes or buying more than five in a 30-day stretch — from purchasing single-family homes [S2]. Funds that already hold homes would have to sell at least 10% of them each year until, ten years after enactment, they hold none, including through parent or subsidiary companies [S2]. It has been referred to the House Financial Services Committee and has not moved since [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, people competing to buy single-family homes would face fewer large institutional buyers bidding on the same houses, and communities with heavy corporate ownership of rentals would see those holdings sold off over a decade, creating more opportunities for owner-occupant buyers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered funds from buying single-family homes beginning 90 days after enactment, reducing competition from institutional buyers at the point of purchase [S2].

Requires funds holding single-family homes on enactment to divest at least 10% of them annually over ten years, converting corporate-owned rentals back toward sale to individual buyers, with holdings through subsidiaries and parents counted to prevent circumvention [S2].

Targets only large players — funds over $500 million in assets, owners of 100 or more homes, or buyers of more than five homes in a 30-day period — leaving small landlords and individual investors untouched [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large investment funds and corporate landlords who own or buy single-family homes would bear the cost: they could no longer add homes (90 days after enactment) and would have to sell at least 10% of their current single-family holdings each year for ten years, covering homes held through parent or subsidiary companies as well [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporate landlords and investment funds

drawbacks.text: The bill has no cosponsors from either party, giving it no visible base of support in the House [S3].

A forced divestment of at least 10% of holdings per year could push large numbers of corporate-owned rental homes onto the market on a rigid schedule; if local demand is thin, that could disrupt renters in those homes or depress prices in some markets, and if demand is strong, much of the supply may simply pass to other large buyers.

The bill does not limit single-family home buying by other large purchasers — for example, thinly capitalized shell companies or non-fund corporate buyers — so its coverage depends entirely on the fund, REIT, and asset-size definitions it sets [S2].

Institutional owners also supply rental housing; critics of such bans argue that removing them could reduce investment in renovating aging homes, a cost an honest supporter would need to weigh against the benefit to buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For prospective homebuyers, the benefit — fewer large funds competing for the same houses and a decade-long unwind of corporate holdings — is potentially significant in markets with heavy institutional ownership. The main costs are the rigid divestment schedule, which could disrupt renters in sold homes and may not guarantee homes reach owner-occupants, and the bill's narrow definitions, which leave some large buyers untouched. The larger obstacle is not design but momentum: with zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's benefits remain hypothetical [S3] [S4].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat since day one with no hearing, no vote, and no cosigners.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 22, 2026, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, where all further action currently rests [S4].
No cosponsors have joined the bill since introduction [S3].

The bill's coverage test reaches funds with more than $500 million under management, funds owning 100 or more single-family homes, or funds that bought more than five homes in any 30-day period in the prior year, and it counts holdings through parent and subsidiary companies [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo persists: large institutional owners of single-family rental homes face no new restrictions, and ordinary buyers continue competing with them for houses. Who comes out ahead of the bill itself will not be known unless it advances [S4].

for.name: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar large funds and investment companies from buying single-family homes and require a 10-year phased divestment of existing holdings [S2].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls have occurred; the bill's single sponsor is a Republican with no cosponsors from either party so far [S3].

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (private funds and REITs)
industries.note: These firms — including private-equity-backed single-family rental operators and single-family rental REITs — would be barred from adding homes and forced to sell at least 10% of their holdings annually for ten years. Their business model relies on buying houses that individual buyers would otherwise bid on, so their interest in this bill runs against prospective homebuyers.

industries.industry: Large asset managers and private equity real estate
industries.note: The bill reaches funds above $500 million in assets and counts holdings through parent and subsidiary structures, limiting easy workarounds, though funds just below the size and ownership thresholds would remain free to keep buying homes.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors nearly a week after introduction and no committee action beyond referral, the bill is on the standard path of most House bills, which die in committee without a hearing or vote. Advancing would require the Financial Services Committee to take it up and leadership to schedule floor time, neither of which is currently indicated [S3] [S4].
